questions.problem: Given a rectangular solid, find the differential $\text{d}V$ for the volume $V$ of the rectangular solid if the lengths of the sides are $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1.$
questions.worked_solution:
The volume of the rectangular solid is $V=abc.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(a,b,c) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂a})\,\text{d}a+(\frac{∂V}{∂b})\,\text{d}b+(\frac{∂V}{∂c})\,\text{d}c \\  & =bc\,\text{d}a+ac\,\text{d}b+ab\,\text{d}c\end{aligned}
$$

For $a=2,$ $b=5,$ and $c=1,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(2,5,1) & =5\cdot 1\,\text{d}a+2\cdot 1\,\text{d}b+5\cdot 2\,\text{d}c \\  & =5\,\text{d}a+2\,\text{d}b+10\,\text{d}c.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given a right cone, find the differential $\text{d}l$ for the slant height $l$ of the right cone if its base radius is $r=3$ and height $h=4.$
questions.worked_solution:
The slant height of the right cone is $l=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{h}^{2}}.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}l(r,h) & =(\frac{∂l}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂l}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{r}{\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{h}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r+\frac{h}{\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{h}^{2}}}\,\text{d}h\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=3$  and $h=4$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(3,4) & =\frac{3}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}\,\text{d}r+\frac{4}{\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{4}^{2}}}\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{3}{5}\,\text{d}r+\frac{4}{5}\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(xyz),$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(1,1,1)$ to $(2,3,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =\frac{1}{x}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y+\frac{1}{z}\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(1,1,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(1,1,1) & =1\,\text{d}x+1\,\text{d}y+1\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(1+Δx,1+Δy,1+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈Δx+Δy+Δz.
$$

Moving from $(1,1,1)$ to $(2,3,4),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2-1=1, \\ Δy & =3-1=2 \\ Δz & =4-1=3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈Δx+Δy+Δz \\  & ≈1+2+3 \\  & ≈6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ increases by approximately $6.$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y)$ from $(2,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(1.5,1.5).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}x+x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,\frac{\pi }{2}),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,\frac{\pi }{2}) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}x+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Moving from $(2,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(1.5,1.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.5-2=-0.5, \\ Δy & =1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+0\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-0.5)+0\cdot (1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & ≈-0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ decreases by approximately $0.5.$

questions.problem: If $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+4\operatorname{ln}⁡({z}^{3}-y),$ use the differential $\text{d}f$ to estimate the change $Δf$ in the value of $f(x,y,z)$ from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z \\  & =2x\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12{z}^{2}}{{z}^{3}-y})\,\text{d}z\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,-3,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(2,-3,1) & =(2\cdot 2)\,\text{d}x-(\frac{4}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{12\cdot {1}^{2}}{{1}^{3}-(-3)})\,\text{d}z \\  & =4\,\text{d}x-\,\text{d}y+3\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,-3+Δy,1+Δz),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈4\,Δx-\,Δy+3\,Δz.
$$

Moving from $(2,-3,1)$ to $(1,-2,2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1-2=-1, \\ Δy & =-2-(-3)=1 \\ Δz & =2-1=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈4\,Δx-1\,Δy+3\,Δz \\  & ≈4\cdot (-1)-1\cdot 1+3\cdot 1 \\  & ≈-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y,z)$ decreases by approximately $-2.$

$$

Moving from $(0,4)$ to $(-1,5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =-1-0=-1, \\ Δy & =5-4=1.\end{aligned}

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\,Δx+\frac{1}{4}\,Δy \\  & ≈0\cdot (-1)+\frac{1}{4}\cdot (1) \\  & ≈0.25.\end{aligned}

$$

So, if we move to the point $(4+Δx,\frac{\pi }{2}+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx-2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt{3.9}\operatorname{cos}⁡(1.5)=f(3.9,1.5),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3.9,1.5).$

Moving from $(4,\frac{\pi }{2})$ to $(3.9,1.5),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3.9-4=-0.1, \\ Δy & =1.5-\frac{\pi }{2}≈-0.070796.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

questions.problem: Estimate $(1.81)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.91)$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡y$ at the point $(2,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡y\,\text{d}x+\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(2,1),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(1)\,\text{d}x+\frac{2}{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =0\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,1+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈0\,Δx+2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
(1.81)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.91)=f(1.81,0.91),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(1.81,0.91).$

Moving from $(2,1)$ to $(1.81,0.91),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =1.81-2=-0.19, \\ Δy & =0.91-1=-0.09.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈0\cdot (-0.19)+2\cdot (-0.09) \\  & ≈0-0.18 \\  & ≈-0.18.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ decreases by about $0.18.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(1.81,0.91) & ≈f(2,1)-0.18 \\ (1.81)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.91) & ≈2\operatorname{ln}⁡1-0.18 \\  & ≈0-0.18 \\  & ≈-0.18.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Estimate ${e}^{(0.3)(2.15)}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{xy}$ at the point $(0,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =y{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}x+x{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(0,2),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =2\cdot {e}^{0\cdot 2}\,\text{d}x+0\cdot {e}^{0\cdot 2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(0+Δx,2+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈2\,Δx+0\,Δy.
$$

Note that 

$$
{e}^{(0.3)(2.15)}=f(0.3,2.15),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(0.3,2.15).$

Moving from $(0,2)$ to $(0.3,2.15),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =0.3-0=0.3, \\ Δy & =2.15-2=0.15.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈2\cdot (0.3)+0\cdot (0.15) \\  & ≈0.6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.6.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(0.3,2.15) & ≈f(0,2)+0.6 \\ {e}^{(0.3)(2.15)} & ≈{e}^{(0)(2)}+0.6 \\  & ≈1+0.6 \\  & ≈1.6\,.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & ={e}^{0}\,\text{d}x+2\cdot {e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+2\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(2+Δx,0+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈1\,Δx+2\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
2.1{e}^{0.2}=f(2.1,0.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(2.1,0.2).$

Moving from $(2,0)$ to $(2.1,0.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2.1-2=0.1, \\ Δy & =0.2-0=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\cdot (0.1)+2\cdot (0.2) \\  & ≈0.1+0.4 \\  & ≈0.5.\end{aligned}

questions.problem: Estimate $\sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150}$ using a differential $\text{d}f$ of the function $f(x,y)=\sqrt[3]{x}+\sqrt{y}$ at the point $(8,144).$ Round your answer to $3$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{3{x}^{2/3}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(8,144),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\frac{1}{3\cdot {8}^{2/3}}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{2\sqrt{144}}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{12}\,\text{d}x+\frac{1}{24}\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(8+Δx,144+Δy),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
Δf≈\frac{1}{12}\,Δx+\frac{1}{24}\,Δy
$$

Note that 

$$
\sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150}=f(10,150),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(10,150).$

Moving from $(8,144)$ to $(10,150),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =10-8=2, \\ Δy & =150-144=6.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈\frac{1}{12}(2)+\frac{1}{24}(6) \\  & ≈\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{4} \\  & ≈\frac{5}{12} \\  & ≈0.417.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.417.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(10,150) & ≈f(8,144)+0.417 \\ \sqrt[3]{10}+\sqrt{150} & ≈\sqrt[3]{8}+\sqrt{144}+0.417 \\  & ≈2+12+0.417 \\  & ≈14.417.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Computing a Differential in a Geometrical Context
canonical_examples.problem: Given a cone, find the differential $\textrm d V$ for the volume $V$ of the cone if the radius is $r=6$ and the height is $h = 3.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The volume of the cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3} \pi r^2h.$ Let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(r,h) & =(\frac{∂V}{∂r})\,\text{d}r+(\frac{∂V}{∂h})\,\text{d}h \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\pi rh\,\text{d}r+\frac{1}{3}\pi {r}^{2}\,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

For $r=6$ and $h=3,$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}V(6,3) & =\frac{2}{3}\pi \cdot 6\cdot 3\,\text{d}r+\frac{1}{3}\pi \cdot {6}^{2}\,\text{d}h \\  & =12\pi \,\text{d}r+12\pi \,\text{d}h.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Using Differentials to Approximate the Change in a Multivariable Function
canonical_examples.problem: If $f (x, y) = xe^y ,$ use the differential $\textrm d f$ to estimate the change $\Delta f$ in the value of $f(x, y)$ from $(5,0)$ to $(2,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={e}^{y}\,\text{d}x+x{e}^{y}\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $(5,0),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(5,0) & ={e}^{0}\,\text{d}x+5{e}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & =1\,\text{d}x+5\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(5 + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx 1 \, \Delta x + 5 \, \Delta y.
$$

Moving from $(5,0)$ to $(2,1),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =2-5=-3, \\ Δy & =1-0=1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈1\,Δx+5\,Δy \\  & ≈1\cdot (-3)+5\cdot (1) \\  & ≈2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $f(x,y)$ increases by approximately $2.$

Example: 
                    Using Differentials to Approximate the Value of a Function
canonical_examples.problem: Estimate $\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)$ using a differential of the function $f(x,y) = \sin x + \cos y$ at the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, let's find the differential:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

At the point $\left( \pi, 0 \right),$ the differential is

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi \,\text{d}x-\operatorname{sin}⁡0\,\text{d}y \\  & =-1\,\text{d}x+0\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

So, if we move to the point $(\pi + \Delta x, 0 + \Delta y),$ then we can approximate the change in $f$ as

$$
\Delta f \approx  -1  \,  \Delta x + 0  \,  \Delta y
$$

Note that 

$$
\sin (3) + \cos (0.2)= f(3,0.2),
$$

so we want to move to the point $(3,0.2).$

Moving from $(\pi, 0)$ to $(3,0.2),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δx & =3-\pi ≈-0.141, \\ Δy & =0.2-0=0.2.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf & ≈-1(-0.141)+0(0.2) \\  & ≈0.141.\end{aligned}
$$

This means that the value of $f$ increases by about $0.141.$ Consequently, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(3,0.2) & ≈f(\pi ,0)+0.141 \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(3)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0.2) & ≈\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+0.141 \\  & ≈0+1+0.141 \\  & ≈1.141.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
The **differential** of a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ is denoted $\textrm df(x,y)$ and represents the infinitesimal change in the function value that occurs when the inputs $x$ and $y$ are changed by infinitesimal amounts $\textrm dx$ and $\textrm dy.$

The formula for the differential comes from the multivariable chain rule, which can be expressed as

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that the differential can be extended to any number of variables. For example, for a three-variable function $f(x,y,z),$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y,z) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y+(\frac{∂f}{∂z})\,\text{d}z.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Approximating Change Using Differentials
tutorials.problem:
Given a multivariable function $f(x,y),$ the differential

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{d}f(x,y) & =(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,\text{d}x+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

tells us how infinitesimal changes in $x$ and $y,$ denoted $\textrm dx$ and $\textrm dy,$ result in an infinitesimal change in $f,$ denoted $\textrm df.$

Consequently, we can use the differential to *approximate* the change in $f$ as we move from one point to another. If we move from a point $(x,y)$ to a point $(x + \Delta x, y + \Delta y),$ then the approximate change in $f$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}Δf(x,y) & ≈(\frac{∂f}{∂x})\,Δx+(\frac{∂f}{∂y})\,Δy.\end{aligned}
$$

The above formula is very similar to the differential formula, except the $\textrm d$'s are replaced with $\Delta$'s. The $\textrm d$'s refer to infinitesimal changes, while the $\Delta$'s refer to changes that can actually be measured.
